cards.title: Show HN: Steal My Bitcoin

depth.text: someone hid a **Bitcoin key** on a server and challenged people to **steal the wallet**

The challenge page says the key is reachable through the PHP user account’s **print-flag binary**. One commenter says the setup is **not vulnerable to PHP2SHELL**; another claims to have a working RCE but **won’t demonstrate it**, fearing it could leak what they built.

cards.title: The Goose Programming Language

depth.text: someone made **Goose**, a language where the compiler assigns **data stacks** for memory

One commenter says Goose suits programs with a **fixed number of growable memory regions**, but another asks how it handles arbitrary numbers of changing-size values without a heap. A commenter also warns that, with **no garbage collection**, stacks can keep growing even when old data is no longer used.

cards.camps: Two camps: skeptics say a fixed set of stacks may not handle arbitrary, changing-size values and argue a proper heap may be needed; supporters say Goose is fine for programs that can set the number of growable memory regions in advance.

As long as you can statically specify the number of growable memory regions, you can use Goose. cards.title: We should be more ambitious with the software we build

depth.text: someone says **AI** makes **ambitious projects** practical, so developers can build things they once ruled out

The writer says this set of tools took a **low single-digit number of hours**, including a regex engine tuned to his workloads, a faster ripgrep fork, and a Rust interpreter. Yossi Kreinin's reply warns that most people should be less ambitious with AI-built software if they lack **clear checks** or struggle to understand what it builds.

cards.camps: Two camps: advocates say AI makes once-impractical projects feasible; skeptics say most people should be less ambitious without clear checks and the ability to understand what they build.

cards.title: America has lost 200k of jobs in media, film and the arts. How much is AI?

depth.text: someone asks how much **AI** is to blame for **job losses** across America’s creative industries

Nearly half of the losses were in **movie and sound recording**, including Hollywood, but the article says **AI’s role is hard to separate** from consolidation, offshoring and social media’s rise. It warns that creative industries could face a **business-model collapse** like newspapers did.
data: creative-industry jobs lost in four years
creative-industry jobs lost in the last year

cards.title: GPU-unlock: FP/BF16 instruction issue rate on Nvidia 3000's cards

depth.text: someone built a **Linux tool** that unlocks **faster math** on some Nvidia GeForce cards

The project says its module doubles **FP/BF16 FMA instruction issue speed** on GA102, GA103, GA104 and GA106 cards, loading before the unmodified NVIDIA driver. It reports faster **LLM prefill**, while decode and INT8 work stay about the same; commenters dispute what gets unlocked and how widely it has been tested.

cards.camps: Two camps: the project says it unlocks FP/BF16 instruction speed across four GPU families; one commenter says the claim is really about FP32 and says they have seen reports only for 3090/3090 Ti cards.

cards.title: Danish Government silently drops plan to dump MS Office

depth.text: the Danish digital ministry **quietly dropped** its trial of an **open-source alternative** to Microsoft Office

The pilot began in summer 2025, with **just under 40 ministry employees** testing **Collabora**, supplied by Danish company cBrain. One commenter says a general election put it on **indefinite hold**; no evaluation is planned.

cards.title: Why is AI generated language so hard to understand?

depth.text: researchers found **AI writing** uses more **hard-to-process language**, perhaps because models optimize for tasks beyond communication

All **nine models** used more **inanimate subjects with animate verbs** and low-frequency n-grams than human writing; most also used longer dependencies, more stacked nouns, and more reduced object relatives in conversation. The authors suggest that goals like math, code, and reasoning may favor **information density** over successful communication. They also found that fine-tuning a model with a length penalty led to language that diverged from human-like patterns.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say AI writing is hard to understand because it favors dense information; others say it’s just tedious, or that the bigger issue is whether it’s useful to its audience.
terms: inanimate subject with an animate verb

comments.text: As a technical writer, I believe default AI responses are optimized for what people _think_ is good writing rather than what actually is good writing. My guess is years of RLHF optimized for rater's first impressions of how well-written something was. It uses lists! It has headings! It uses fun phrases like 'smoking gun'! It's long and informative! These things are relatively fast and easy to…

One construction I'm surprised the paper doesn't mention (although, to be fair, I'm sure they had plenty of options to choose from... and you have to draw the line somewhere :P) is that LLMs love to use transitive verbs intransitively[0], in a way I almost never see in human writing. At best it makes sentences weirdly ambiguous, at worst it makes them borderline incomprehensible, and it's…

LLMs are showing us that a lot of what we think of as cognition is actually part of the elaborate symbol system which is Language, as opposed to a property of "mind" (either biologically or artificially instantiated.) LLM-generated text is hard to understand because while it's perfectly good language that follows valid cognitive and informational patterns, it does not reflect the intent or mental…

Consider too that AI training corpuses include vast amounts of commercial speech which is designed to numb the critical faculties and produce action; likewise they include numerous opinion articles, which are designed to persuade and often leverage rhetorical fallacies, whether cynically or as a reflection of an author's imperfect thought process.

We note that the model was not directly instructed to use compressed or dense language, and was not directly given information about the availability of syntactic…

depth.text: Goose is a **systems language** that stays **memory safe** without a heap or lifetime annotations

Goose stores dynamic values inline on **compiler-managed data stacks** and frees them when their scope ends; it also compiles to one C file. Its repository benchmarks report **3.3x the speed** of idiomatic C++, 1.16x hand-optimized C++, and 1.12x the best safe Rust, using **less memory**.

cards.title: Dream-1

depth.text: someone made a robot model that can control **new robots** doing **tasks it has never seen**

Dream Labs says **Dream-1** works through a public API with **bimanual robots** using parallel grippers, without robot-specific fine-tuning or demonstrations. It costs **$3 per hour** ($2 per hour for Dream-1-flash), but the post warns it isn't validated for safety-critical use.

cards.camps: Two camps: some are excited about robots taking on household chores; others say the demos don't show useful real-world automation yet.

comments.text: Tested one prompt in the playground ("Move the elephant next to the ball") and this is the generated recorded video link: https://dreamlabs.ai/playground/?play=a05f0e641559490e#sim

This is all very cool and something I would like to play with. However I also can’t mentally bridge this over to the actual automation, manufacturing, and warehouse work I’ve been involved with throughout my career. Everything about this looks optimized for getting-started tasks to play around with, but I’m left feeling that it’s not the right fit or even a good starting point for real automation…

Obviously AI written text. At least there is real content here, however I do find the order and the way in which it was written and portrayed to have a heavy AI smell. That is, it's hard to read and follow the clean narrative, it isn't written the way a human who was trying to convince another human would write, and is less effective because of it.

This post feels really weird, DreamLabs isn’t some well known project like Anthropic or OpenAI and Dream-1 wasn’t really an awaited release. But somehow this was pushed to the front page of HN before receiving a single comment with a title reminiscent of a major LLM release. Like I can only find 1 other reference historically to this lab and nobody noticed it or cared.

I don't like the direction this is going in - so a third party is going to be able to control a robot in my house? we shouldn't aim for economies of scale on this problem as there are massive negative externalities attached to it. Hopefully, a chinese lab will release an open source version soon.

glossary.PHP: PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor; a language people use to make websites work.
glossary.PHP2SHELL: The name used here for PHP-related flaws that could let an attacker run commands on a server.
glossary.RCE: Remote Code Execution: a flaw that lets an attacker make a computer run their commands from somewhere else.
glossary.honeypot: A computer set up to attract attacks so people can watch what attackers do.
glossary.binary: A program file a computer can run.
glossary.POC: Proof of Concept: a small test or demo that checks whether an idea can work.
glossary.CVE: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: a standard ID assigned to a publicly known security flaw so people can refer to the same issue.
glossary.CLI: Command-Line Interface: a way to control a computer by typing commands instead of clicking buttons.
glossary.data stack: A dedicated area of memory where a program keeps data; Goose uses several areas assigned by the compiler.
glossary.heap: Memory a program can request as it runs, useful when it doesn’t know in advance how much space its data will need.
glossary.garbage collection: Automatic cleanup that frees memory the program is no longer using.
glossary.dynamically sized: Able to grow or shrink while a program is running.
glossary.regex engine: Software that checks text against patterns, such as finding words in a chosen format.
glossary.ripgrep: A search tool for finding text inside files.
glossary.Rust interpreter: Software that runs Rust code by carrying out its instructions.
glossary.agentic loop: A cycle where an AI tries a task, checks what happened, and tries again.
glossary.benchmark: A test people use to compare how well different tools do a task.
glossary.offshoring: Moving work to another country instead of doing it where the company is based.
glossary.consolidation: When businesses combine or are bought, leaving fewer, larger companies in an industry.
glossary.paywall: A website barrier that asks you to pay before reading an article.
glossary.BF16: Brain Floating Point 16: a format for storing the numbers a model works with.
glossary.FP32: Floating-point 32: a way for computers to represent numbers during calculations.
glossary.FMA: Fused multiply-add: an instruction that multiplies two numbers and adds a third in one step.
glossary.instruction issue rate: How quickly a GPU can start the calculation instructions it is given.
glossary.LLM prefill: Large language model prefill: the step where an AI reads your prompt before generating its reply.
glossary.kernel module: A small piece of software that runs inside Linux and adds behavior related to the computer's hardware.
glossary.open source: Software whose code is shared so other people can inspect, run, or change it.
glossary.digital sovereignty: A country’s ability to control the technology it relies on instead of depending on outside providers.
glossary.mail merge: A way to make many personalized letters or labels from one document and a list of names.
glossary.track-changes: A document feature that shows edits made by reviewers.
glossary.CRUD apps: Create, Read, Update, Delete: a basic app for adding, viewing, changing, and removing records.
glossary.low-frequency n-gram: A short run of words or word pieces that appears only rarely in the writing being studied.
glossary.inanimate subject with an animate verb: A sentence where a thing, rather than a person or animal, is described as doing an action.
glossary.object relative: A phrase that tells you about a thing by saying what someone did to it, as in “the book that I read.”
glossary.information density: How much information is packed into a small amount of writing.
glossary.fine-tuning: Training an already-built model a bit more on examples for a particular job.
glossary.RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: a way to train an AI by having people rate its answers.
glossary.transitive verb used intransitively: Using a verb without an object, even though it normally says what the action affects.
glossary.heap allocator: A system that hands a program separate chunks of memory when it asks for them.
glossary.lifetime annotations: Extra marks in code that tell the compiler how long a reference is allowed to stay usable.
glossary.garbage collector: A part of a program that finds memory it no longer needs so that space can be reused.
glossary.World Action Model: A robot AI that learns to predict what it will see and what actions would make that happen.
glossary.zero-shot: Trying a task or using a robot without first giving the model examples for that exact task or robot.
glossary.parallel grippers: Robot hands that grip an object by closing two sides toward each other.
glossary.API: Application Programming Interface: a way for one program to ask another for information or actions.
glossary.IK solver: Inverse kinematics solver: software that works out how a robot's joints need to move to put its hand somewhere.
